findings.finding: My current finding is that the condition on a shifty function α is equivalent to the existence of a Laurent polynomial B_rev(x)=∑b_jx^{-j} such that A(x)·B_rev(x)=x^k+x^l, where A(x)=∑_{i=0}^8 a_i x^i. Thus α is shifty iff the binomial x^k+x^l factors over ℤ into a polynomial of degree ≤8 and a Laurent polynomial with finite support. This reduces the problem to counting integer factorizations of x^k+x^l with one factor of bounded degree.

My current finding is that the condition “∃ β, k≠l such that Sₙ(α)⋆β=1_{k,l}(n)” is equivalent to the existence of Laurent polynomials A(z)=∑_{i=0}^8α(i)z^i and B(z)=∑_tβ(t)z^{-t} with integer coefficients satisfying A(z)·B(z)=z^k+z^l.  Thus A(z) must divide z^k+z^l in ℤ[z,z⁻¹], i.e. A(z)=±z^m·d(z) where d(z) is a divisor of z^d+1 with d=|k−l|.  This reduces the counting problem to enumerating all integer polynomials of degree ≤8 that divide some cyclotomic polynomial z^d+1 (up to a unit z^m).

My current finding is that a shifty function must have support exactly on the set $\{0,\dots,8\}$ and its values $a_i$ must satisfy that there exists a finite integer sequence $b_j$ and two distinct shifts $k,l$ with  
$$\sum_{i=0}^8 a_i\,b_{i-n}=\begin{cases}1,&n=k,l\\0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$  
This is equivalent to requiring that the cross‑correlation of $a$ and $b$ has exactly two nonzero entries. The problem reduces to finding integer vectors $a\in\mathbb Z^9$ for which such a $b$ exists. The key insight is that $b$ can be chosen to have support only where $a$ is nonzero, so the system of equations is finite. This sets the stage for enumerating all possible $a$ by solving a finite linear system over $\mathbb Z$.

My current finding is that the problem reduces to counting integer polynomials $A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^8a_i x^i$ that can be multiplied by some integer Laurent polynomial $B(x)=\sum_{j}b_jx^j$ to give exactly two monomials: $A(x)B(x)=x^k+x^l$ with $k\neq l$.  Thus each shifty $\alpha$ corresponds to a factorisation of a binomial $x^k+x^l$ into a degree‑≤8 polynomial with integer coefficients and another Laurent polynomial.  The count of shifty functions equals the number of such $A(x)$, independent of the particular $B(x)$ or the shift indices $k,l$.

My current finding is that the problem reduces to factoring the binomial \(z^k+z^l\) in the Laurent polynomial ring \(\mathbb Z[z,z^{-1}]\).  
Since \(\alpha\) has support in \(\{0,\dots,8\}\), its generating polynomial \(A(z)=\sum_{i=0}^8\alpha(i)z^i\) has degree ≤ 8.  
The cross‑correlation condition is equivalent to the existence of a Laurent polynomial \(B(z)\) with \(A(z)B(z)=z^k+z^l\).  
Thus every shifty \(\alpha\) corresponds to an integer divisor \(A(z)\) of some binomial \(z^k+z^l\) with \(\deg A\le8\).  
This bijection allows us to count shifty functions by enumerating all such divisors.

My current finding is that any $\alpha$ with exactly two non‑zero entries equal to 1 (and all other values 0) satisfies the shifty condition.  
Indeed, choose $\beta=\delta_{r}$ (the Kronecker delta at $r$). Then $S_n(\alpha)\star\beta=\alpha(n+r)$, which equals 1 only for $n$ such that $n+r$ equals one of the two positions of the 1’s in $\alpha$, and 0 elsewhere.  Thus all such $\alpha$ are shifty.

My current finding is that a shifty function α is equivalent to the existence of a factorization of a binomial $x^p+x^q$ (with $p<q$) into two integer polynomials where one factor $A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^8 a_i x^i$ has degree ≤8.  Since $x^p+x^q=x^p(1+x^{q-p})$, a trivial factorization is $A(x)=\pm x^p$ and $D(x)=1\pm x^{q-p}$.  Thus any α whose support corresponds to a monomial factor $x^p$ (i.e., all $a_i=0$ except possibly one non‑zero $a_p$) is shifty.  The challenge is to determine whether any other non‑monomial $A(x)$ of degree ≤8 can also factor $x^p+x^q$ into two integer polynomials.

My current finding is that the convolution condition forces the support sets \(A=\operatorname{supp}\alpha\subset\{0,\dots,8\}\) and \(B=\operatorname{supp}\beta_{\text{rev}}\) to satisfy \(|A+B|=2\). This is only possible if one of the sets has size 1 and the other size 2 (since \(|A|=|B|=1\) gives \(|A+B|=1\) and \(|A|,|B|\ge3\) gives \(|A+B|\ge3\)). Thus every shifty \(\alpha\) must have exactly one non‑zero entry, and the corresponding \(\beta_{\text{rev}}\) must have exactly two non‑zero entries. This reduces the counting problem to choosing the single index in \(\{0,\dots,8\}\) and the two indices of \(\beta_{\text{rev}}\) (up to a shift that places the two convolution outputs at distinct integers \(k,l\)).

This is equivalent to requiring that the cross‑correlation of $a$ and $b$ has exactly two nonzero entries. Equivalently, \(A(z)=z^m\,P(z)\) where \(P(z)\mid(z^d+1)\) for some \(d=|k-l|>0\) and \(\deg A\le8\).  Thus the problem reduces to counting all integer polynomials of degree ≤8 that divide some cyclotomic polynomial \(z^d+1\).

In particular, \(A(x)\) must be a factor of \(x^l(x^{k-l}+1)\), so it can only involve cyclotomic factors of \(x^{k-l}+1\) together with a possible monomial \(x^m\).  This reduces the problem to counting all primitive divisors of \(x^n+1\) (for \(n\ge1\)) whose degree ≤8, multiplied by any power of \(x\) up to 8.

My current finding is that any shifty function must have exactly one non‑zero entry equal to ±1.  
If α has only one non‑zero value a at position p, we can choose β with support at t=p−k and t=p−l and set β(t)=1/a, giving C(k)=C(l)=1.  
For a≠±1, 1/a is not an integer, so β cannot be integer‑valued.  
Thus α must be of the form α(p)=±1, α(m)=0 for m≠p, with p∈{0,…,8}.  This gives 9×2=18 candidate α’s.  The next step is to check whether any α with ≥2 non‑zero entries can satisfy the conditions.

Conversely, any such divisor A(x) yields a β (via B'(x)=x^kC(x)) giving the required two‑point correlation.  Thus the problem reduces to counting all integer divisors of 1+x^d of degree ≤8.

Thus the problem reduces to counting all monic divisors of some \(x^n+1\) whose degree plus a possible leading monomial \(x^m\) does not exceed 8.  This gives a finite, explicit enumeration of all admissible α.

My current finding is that shifty α can have support size 2 as well as size 1.  
If α has two non‑zero entries a₁,a₂∈{0,…,8} with equal value ±1, choose β with a single non‑zero at b such that β(b)=±1 (the sign opposite to α’s). Then S_{a₁+b}α⋆β=S_{a₂+b}α⋆β=1 and all other n give 0.  
Thus there are C(9,2)=36 pairs of support indices, each with two sign choices, giving 72 α’s, plus the 18 α’s with a single ±1 entry, for a total of 90 shifty functions.

This reduces the counting problem to enumerating all subsets of even cyclotomic polynomials whose total degree ≤ 8 and attaching any monomial factor \(x^s\) with \(s\) filling the remaining degree.

This forces the intersection \(\bigcap_{a\in A}\{k-a,l-a\}\) to be non‑empty, so all \(a\in A\) lie in \(\{k-b_0,l-b_0\}\) for some common \(b_0\).  Hence \(A\) can contain at most two distinct values, and similarly \(B\) can contain at most two.  This drastically limits the possible \(\alpha\) to those with support size ≤2.

The admissible cyclotomic factors are \(\Phi_2,\Phi_4,\Phi_6,\Phi_8,\Phi_{10},\Phi_{12},\Phi_{14},\Phi_{16},\Phi_{18},\Phi_{20},\Phi_{24},\Phi_{30}\) with degrees \(1,2,2,4,4,4,6,8,6,8,8,8\).
